## What’s Behind Back-to-Back Meltdowns at the F.A.A. and Microsoft


#### Plus, why “birdbrain” is a misnomer.


2026-11-16T06:00:08-05:00


This transcript was created using speech recognition software. While it has been reviewed by human transcribers, it may contain errors. Please review the episode audio before quoting from this transcript and email transcripts@nytimes.com with any questions.


tracy mumford


From “The New York Times,” it’s “The Headlines.” I’m Tracy Mumford. Today’s Monday, November 16. Here’s what we’re covering.


nbc news anchor


Can you guarantee that what happened on Friday won’t happen again, Mr. Secretary?


secretary of transportation sean duffy


Well, first, we have to figure out what happened. Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris, that was doing the work?


tracy mumford


The Secretary of Transportation, Sean Duffy, says that this weekend’s airport chaos was set off by an attempt to update the FAA’s antiquated communications system.


secretary of transportation sean duffy


It goes back 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment, a lack of waving the flag to say, hey, this is a problem. Let’s fix it. Why they didn’t do that? I don’t know.


tracy mumford


After the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, thousands of flights were canceled, stranding tens of thousands of passengers and snarling air travel for days. Here’s what we know so far about what set everything off.


Officials say it began when a contractor upgraded a router in a radio facility in Arkansas — part of an effort to replace old-school copper-wire systems with fiber-optic cable. In the middle of that, officials noticed that the facility and another recently upgraded one in Texas, had started to ping the FAA communications network and an abnormally high rate, basically overwhelming the system with data. According to the FAA’s chief technology officer, that set off failures in other parts of the network and forced officials to declare the ground stop.


karoun demirjian


There are vulnerabilities in the FAA’s telecoms and infrastructure systems that mean that when something goes wrong, there isn’t necessarily a buffer or a cushion there. The FAA Administrator, Brian Bedford, on Saturday morning said there are no backups to the backup.


tracy mumford


Karoun Demirjian covers aviation and transportation for “The Times.” She says there have been concerns about how the Trump administration is handling the much-needed effort to modernize the country’s air traffic control network. Earlier this fall, a nonpartisan government watchdog warned that the government was moving too quickly to overhaul such a fragile system.


karoun demirjian


It’s a major project. It’s something that, there is bipartisan agreement, has to be tackled. But there is disagreement about whether the style in which this administration is tackling this and the way in which they are looking at these potential points of failure or actual points of failure, as we saw on Friday, is really adequately taking these risks into consideration.


\[INTRIGUING MUSIC\]


tracy mumford


Over the weekend, Duffy called on Congress to fast track $50 billion in new funding for air traffic control upgrades by the end of the year. That’s a drastically larger sum than he’s asked for before, and it drew sharp criticism from some lawmakers. Two top Democrats on House panels overseeing the FAA put out a statement pointing out that the agency still hasn’t spent the majority of the funds Congress already gave it for modernization.


This week, President Trump is headed to China for a meeting that was intended to be about extending a trade war truce, but now has a new twist.


reporter


Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him?


president donald trump


No, I don’t think so. I mean, maybe. I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man.


tracy mumford


Trump will be making the trip with the shock of Jensen Huang’s resignation from NVIDIA still fresh. And despite the geopolitical storm around it, Trump has told reporters he doesn’t plan to bring up the issue himself of Huang and his affair with a woman who US intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy.


stephen smith


Should he have stepped down?


president donald trump


\[SIGHS\] Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.


tracy mumford


The president has said he doesn’t remember being briefed on the intelligence and has downplayed concerns about it. But my colleague, David Pierson, who covers China, says the situation has underscored what’s happening between the two countries behind the scenes.


david pierson


Under Xi, China has intensified its spying operations. It has transformed its spy agency, known as the Ministry of State Security, from really an unsophisticated operation, just dealing with rumors at embassy dinner parties, to using AI tools, to employing the public to help them in all intelligence gathering now. At the same time, the United States is also stepped up its resources in spying on China, recognizing that it has to expand the scope of its intelligence gathering to include Chinese businesses, because so much of the competition between China and the United States is economic today.


So on the surface, it looks like the two leaders are helping stabilize relations. And on some level, it really is like that. But just beneath the surface, there’s still a furious spy war going on between the two countries.


\[CONTEMPLATIVE MUSIC\]


tracy mumford


Now, two other quick updates on the Trump administration. First, federal officials have pushed back a key deadline that affects millions of people on Medicaid. As of January 1, many Medicaid recipients were going to have to complete forms proving they were working or volunteering to keep their insurance coverage. And a lot of hospitals had gone into overdrive, trying to alert patients to the upcoming changes in time. Now, the administration says states can wait until this summer to start enforcing the work rules, acknowledging how difficult it’s been to build new software systems to track the stricter eligibility requirements. Still, the eventual rollout of the new rules is expected to have a widespread impact on patients and health care systems. According to a government estimate, over the next few years, the rules will mean that about five million Americans lose their health insurance, including many who get tripped up by the new paperwork challenges.


\[UPBEAT MUSIC\]


And a new survey out today shows that international student enrollment at American universities is continuing to plunge, as Trump administration policies appear to be driving foreign students away. According to data from the Institute of International Education, new international student enrollment dropped by 15 percent this fall. That’s on top of an 18 percent drop last year. While the US is still the top destination for international students worldwide, changing visa policies and fears over the White House’s crackdown on immigrants have made some students decide to go elsewhere for their higher education.


That is already taking a major toll on universities’ bottom line. Many international students pay full tuition, effectively subsidizing the cost for Americans. And schools around the US have already cited a loss of revenue from international students as the reason they’ve had to lay off employees, cut budgets, and close programs.


\[VIBRANT MUSIC\]


News now on the other recent tech outage that left people scrambling over the past few days — not the FAA, but Microsoft.


pbd pocast


Outlook is down. Exchange Online, Teams down. Copilot is down.


tracy mumford


Starting on Thursday, millions of people worldwide were cut off from email, video meetings, and other features.


tiktoker


I literally just tried to open up an email on Outlook. And Outlook looked at me like, are you stupid, Warren?


tracy mumford


The technical issues ballooned to affect people across the US and dozens of other countries. Singapore’s tax authorities couldn’t receive messages. Pharmacies in Britain struggled to fill prescriptions. And Australian intelligence and police forces said their operations were also affected.


By Saturday, the tech giant was able to fully restore its services. Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber attack or related to artificial intelligence. Instead, the company said that the problems began during an upgrade, similar to the FAA.


Experts say those two upgrades gone awry highlight how fragile many digital systems actually are, in everything from banking to health care to transportation. A lot of them rely on a combination of new and old hardware, plus software that needs frequent updating. Over the years, they’ve almost become like geological formations, with new layers piling on top of old ones.


Upset that delicate balance, though, and the whole system can come crashing down. Microsoft has yet to provide a clear answer for what exactly went wrong during the update. It’s promised to publish a full report identifying the, quote, “root cause” of the outage.


\[TENSE MUSIC\]


And finally, humans owe birds an apology. For a long time, scholars studying birds looked at their small brains and concluded they weren’t all that bright, hence the term “birdbrain,” not a compliment. But evidence has been increasingly piling up that there’s a lot more happening in there than anyone was giving birds credit for. For example, some species are capable of distinguishing between cancerous and noncancerous cells. And others can recognize their own image, solve abstract problems, even plan for the future.


And now, new research, published in “The Journal Science,” shows that crows, specifically, can make decisions faster than humans. The research involved placing crows in front of a swirling mass of dots on a screen, and rewarding them for answering whether the dots were moving to the left or the right. The crows reliably pecked their answers twice as fast as rhesus monkeys or humans. And they did it without compromising accuracy.


One of the authors of the study said he even put all of the people in his lab up against the birds — undergrads, PhDs, postdocs — and they were all too slow for the crows. The research underscores how the avian brain, despite being small, is tuned for rapid processing. The research team suspects it has a lot to do with how risky flying is. In order to stay alive up there, you got to make a lot of decisions really quick.


\[THEME MUSIC\]


Those are “The Headlines.” And before we go, my favorite piece of crow coverage from “The Times” remains the research that showed how good crows are at holding grudges. It turns out they can even pass them down, creating what I guess you would call, multi-generational crow wrath. I’m Tracy Mumford. We’ll be back tomorrow.


Nov. 16, 2026, 6:00 a.m. ET
